common_name: Mme Antoine Mari Rose (Antique Heat-Tolerant Tea Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Mme Antoine Mari is a Tea rose bred in France in the 1900s that has long thrived in the heat and humidity of Deep South gardens with minimal winter protection in zone 7-9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Mme Antoine Mari is a classic Tea rose that has been passed along for generations among Southern rose collectors and preserved by the antique rose movement for its combination of soft blush-pink, high-centered, fragrant blooms with the vigorous, disease-resistant constitution characteristic of old Tea roses. Like other Tea roses it blooms repeatedly through the long, hot growing season and shrugs off the heat and humidity that stress many modern hybrid tea roses, needing little more than a sunny, well-drained spot to perform for decades. Prune lightly to shape after the main spring flush, and expect good resistance to black spot and powdery mildew compared with modern roses bred primarily for cooler climates.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Marie Pavié is an 1888 French polyantha that blooms nearly nonstop through the growing season and has become a favorite low-maintenance landscape rose across the South.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Marie Pavié is a compact, nearly thornless polyantha rose introduced in 1888 that has become one of the most reliable low-maintenance landscape roses in Southern gardens, producing clusters of small, blush-white, sweetly fragrant blooms almost continuously from spring through frost. Its compact, rounded habit and excellent disease resistance make it well suited to borders, mass plantings, and mixed beds without the spraying regimen many modern roses require. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove any dead wood, and expect vigorous rebloom within weeks after each flush is spent or deadheaded.

common_name: Cramoisi Supérieur Rose (Deep-Crimson Antique China Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Cramoisi Supérieur is an 1832 China rose that tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity with minimal winter protection in zone 7-10.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Cramoisi Supérieur, introduced in 1832, is a classic China rose bearing rich, deep crimson, cupped blooms that deepen further in heat rather than fading, produced in flushes almost continuously through the long Gulf South growing season. Like other old China roses it is remarkably tough and disease-resistant, thriving with little more than a sunny spot and occasional shaping, and it has been passed down and rediscovered growing untended at old homesites across the South for generations. Its manageable size fits foundation plantings and mixed borders as easily as historic rose collections, and it needs only light pruning after each bloom flush to encourage continued repeat flowering.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a trellis, fence, or arbor to support the climbing canes; Rêve d'Or is an 1869 Noisette rose that thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf South gardens.

directions: Plant at the base of a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence in well-drained soil in full sun, tying in the vigorous climbing canes as they grow. Rêve d'Or, introduced in 1869, is a classic climbing Noisette rose bearing clusters of fragrant, golden-apricot to buff-yellow blooms flushed with warm color, repeating through the growing season on a vigorous, nearly thornless plant well suited to Southern heat and humidity. Noisette roses were developed in Charleston, South Carolina in the early 1800s and remain some of the best-adapted climbing roses for the Deep South, tolerating the heat, humidity, and disease pressure that limit many modern climbers. Train canes horizontally along a support to encourage the most flowering laterals, and prune lightly after the main flush to maintain shape and promote repeat bloom.

common_name: Peggy Martin Rose (The Katrina Rose, Thornless Found Climber)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a fence, arbor, or trellis for the vigorous climbing canes; Peggy Martin is a thornless found rose famous for surviving weeks of brackish floodwater in a New Orleans garden after Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

directions: Plant at the base of a sturdy fence, arbor, or trellis in well-drained soil in full sun, and let the long, nearly thornless canes ramble and climb. Peggy Martin became famous across the Gulf South as the 'Katrina Rose' after a specimen in a Plaquemines Parish, Louisiana garden survived two weeks submerged in brackish Hurricane Katrina floodwater and leafed out again the following spring, after which cuttings were propagated and distributed to raise funds for hurricane-ravaged gardens and parks. It produces large sprays of small, deep pink, mildly fragrant blooms in a spectacular once-a-year spring flush, on a vigorous, once-blooming climber that is exceptionally tough, disease-resistant, and tolerant of poor or even storm-damaged soil. Give it strong support to climb, and prune only lightly right after the spring bloom to control size, since it flowers on old wood.

common_name: Souvenir de St. Anne's Rose (Sparse-Petaled Antique Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Souvenir de St. Anne's is a sparse-petaled sport of the Bourbon rose Souvenir de la Malmaison, discovered in an Irish garden and long grown in warm-climate heirloom rose collections.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun. Souvenir de St. Anne's is a distinctive sport of the famous Bourbon rose Souvenir de la Malmaison, bearing the same soft blush-pink coloring but with far fewer petals, giving each bloom a loose, semi-double, almost single-rose appearance that reveals its golden stamens. It repeats reliably through the growing season and, like other Bourbon roses, performs well in the heat and humidity of Southern gardens with good disease resistance for an antique variety. Its more compact, well-behaved habit compared with many old Bourbons makes it a manageable choice for a mixed border or heirloom rose collection. Prune lightly after each bloom flush to encourage continued repeat flowering through the season.
